title: New Fusion connection management on Snowflake and BigQuery produces timeouts (threads config is ignored)
body:
**Describe the bug**
`dbtf run --help` shows --threads defaults to `max_cpu`, not the profile value:
```
--threads <THREADS>    The number of threads to use [Run with --threads 0 to use max_cpu [default: max_cpu]]
```

profiles.yml sets threads: 4, but dbtf run ignores that, causing severe warehouse contention. Core correctly reads the profile and uses 4 threads.

**What version of dbt Fusion is this bug in? (find out by running `dbt --version`)**
2.0.0-preview.120

**Is this a discrepancy between the dbt Fusion Engine and dbt Core? Check one.**
- [x] YES
- [ ] NO

**Expected behavior**
Fusions should read threads from profiles.yml

**Operating System and CPU Type:**
Linux 6.6.87.2 (WSL2), x86_64, 22 CPUs

comments.author: dataders
comments.body:
hey @schwericke what data platform are you on?

have you seen the recent Fusion-specific addition to the [Using threads docs page](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/running-a-dbt-project/using-threads#fusion-engine-thread-optimization)?

we _could_ respect user threads, but our current philosophy is that users shouldn't have to think about it and dbt should handle warehouse concurrency well.

Admittedly, we have improvements to handle it better. For example, if you're on Snowflake, we did ship a change in preview.120 that we know opens too many connections. I'd be curious if you were to update to a newer version, if you see any improvement.

comments.author: radian21
comments.body:
Thanks @eliasdefaria and @felipecrv. Adding some more context. My understanding from the [dbt docs](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/running-a-dbt-project/using-threads?version=1.12#fusion-engine-thread-optimization) is that, by design, fusion seeks to abstract away the need for the engineer to worry about setting the thread count unlike dbt-core and tries to optimize this internally. 

The docs state for Snowflake:

> Fusion ignores user-set threads and automatically optimizes parallelism for maximum performance.
The only supported override is threads: 1, which can also help resolve timeout issues if set.

This statement is not quite clear. What is the intended behavior when the supported override of `threads: 1` is used in the profile? Does fusion try to truly single-thread the processing to control timeouts in this case? If so, I've seen this fail when running many models even on a 2XL warehouse (much larger than I normally use). I've witnessed continued dbt1308 timeouts even with 1 thread configured.

Or is the design intent of `threads: 1` something else - more an an *override flag*? Does this setting trigger fusion to attempt a different strategy that remains multi-threaded to "help resolve timeout issues"?

Thanks for your insights and help to resolve this issue.

comments.author: felipecrv
comments.body:
First of all, Fusion needs improvement here. There is *an issue* and I'm working on a fix right now. I don't think the docs would be able to explain all the details.

## The issue

`threads` is a setting from dbt Core that leaks implementation details. It assumes that limiting threads is possible and by doing so can limit the number of connections which really is the goal of the setting.

Fusion uses `tokio`. Tokio uses thread-pools for everything. When you dispatch work (async/await) it can go anywhere (any thread).

There's an async pool with a fixed size proportional to number of CPUs. These threads are supposed to run non-blocking operations. They are supposed to quickly consume short duration tasks and schedule short duration tasks.

When you need to run jinja, open a file (`tokio::fs`), do something on the database, you must wrap the work in a `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. This turns blocking work into a quick async task that simply sends the work to the second thread-pool. This thread pool can have up to 512 threads. The number must be high because every blocking operation uses it.

Limiting these threads would reduce the number of connections used by Fusion but would also slow down everything in a bad way.

## The fix

Interpret `threads` to mean the "maximum number of connections". The difficulty here is now enforcing the limit.

Blocking when a new connection is requested would slow down operations indefinitely (minutes), pushing tokio to create more threads in the blocking pool. The more threads you have, the harder it is for the threads to reuse an existing connection.

We need to track the number of connections (easy) then, at the dbt tasks level, signal backpressure to `tokio` instead scheduling more work when connections are the limit.

Connections should jump between threads now, but we need to be careful to not interleave multiple nodes on the same connection.

A challenge here is that nodes are black boxes containing arbitrary jinja code. We might have to overestimate backpressure, but still better than limiting threads at a global level.

comments.author: robinsaa
comments.body:
Running into the same issue on Snowflake — adding detail here as it may differ slightly from the Redshift case above.

**Environment**
- dbt Fusion (latest) - Cloud
- Snowflake
- ~3,000+ models and tests

**Symptoms**

After upgrading from dbt Core to Fusion, runs that previously completed reliably now intermittently fail with:

```
timeout after MMmSs and 8 attempts. HTTP Status: 503. Hanging?
```

Checking Snowflake query history, I can see 20+ queries being submitted simultaneously at peak, which eventually causes Snowflake to start rejecting requests — leading to the 503s above.

**Root cause (suspected)**

The [Fusion docs](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/fusion/about-fusion#thread-management) explicitly state that for Snowflake, the `threads` setting is ignored and Fusion instead automatically optimises parallelism for maximum performance. On a large project like ours, this uncapped parallelism appears to be overloading the warehouse.

With dbt Core, `threads` in `profiles.yml` acted as a hard cap and we never saw this. Fusion's approach works well on smaller projects, but at 3,000+ models it seems to saturate Snowflake's connection limits.

**Request**

Would it be possible to expose a way to cap concurrency for Snowflake, even if Fusion's default is to auto-optimise? Something like a `max_threads` or `fusion_max_parallelism` override in `profiles.yml / dbt cloud` would be a safe escape hatch for large projects hitting warehouse limits.

comments.author: mishamsk
comments.body:
I've merged a change that should properly honor `--threads` as effective cap on connections. It should land in the next release soon.

the changelog line will read:
> Honor the configured threads limit when applying connection backpressure, so runs saturate but do not overshoot connection concurrency
